title: A Category II AIF draws operational bridge borrowings five separate ti
question_text: A Category II AIF draws operational bridge borrowings five separate times in a financial year, each for 20 days and each under 10% of investable funds. Is this within the permitted carve-out?

explanation: Reg. 11 lists conflicts of interest and the procedures to address them among the mandatory PPM disclosures. Guaranteed returns, investor net-worth disclosure and any SEBI merit-approval are not features of the AIF PPM regime.

option_a: A guaranteed minimum internal rate of return promised to the scheme's investors
option_b: Conflicts of interest and the procedures to identify and address them

title: An individual has annual income of one crore twenty lakh rupees and ne
question_text: An individual has annual income of one crore twenty lakh rupees and net worth of five crore fifty lakh rupees, of which three crore is in financial assets. Do they qualify as an accredited investor?

options.text: No, because their annual income is below the two-crore standalone income threshold
No, because their net worth is below the seven-crore-fifty-lakh individual net-worth threshold line
Yes, under the combined route: income of at least 1 crore plus net worth of at least 5 crore
Yes, but only if the value of their primary residence is added into net worth first

explanation: The combined limb requires income of at least one crore AND net worth of at least five crore with at least two crore fifty lakh in financial assets. Income of one crore twenty lakh, net worth of five crore fifty lakh with three crore financial assets satisfies every element. Failing the pure-income or pure-net-worth limb is irrelevant when a limb is met.
option_a: No, because their annual income is below the two-crore standalone income threshold
option_b: No, because their net worth is below the seven-crore-fifty-lakh individual net-worth threshold line

title: A body corporate seeks accreditation. Which single test applies to it?
question_text: A body corporate seeks accreditation. Which single test applies to it?

options.text: Net worth of at least fifty crore rupees, with no financial-assets split imposed
Net worth of at least seven crore fifty lakh rupees, mirroring the individual test
Annual income of at least two crore rupees, mirroring the individual income limb
Net worth of at least fifty crore, of which at least half must be financial assets

explanation: For a body corporate the accreditation test is a flat net worth of at least fifty crore rupees. The seven-crore-fifty-lakh and two-crore figures belong to the individual limbs, and there is no financial-assets split imposed on the corporate test.
option_a: Net worth of at least fifty crore rupees, with no financial-assets split imposed
option_b: Net worth of at least seven crore fifty lakh rupees, mirroring the individual test

option_d: Net worth of at least fifty crore, of which at least half must be financial assets

title: A Category III AIF wishes to offer its investors co-investment through
question_text: A Category III AIF wishes to offer its investors co-investment through a dedicated CIV scheme within the AIF structure. Is this permitted?

No, because co-investment within the AIF structure is prohibited for all categories
No, because the CIV co-investment route is open only to Category I and Category II AIFs

explanation: The Master Circular confines CIV-scheme co-investment to Category I and Category II AIFs, offered to accredited investors, with the CIV scheme ring-fenced and barred from borrowing or leverage. A Category III fund cannot run a CIV co-investment scheme.
option_a: Yes, because any category of AIF may run a CIV co-investment scheme for its investors
option_b: Yes, provided the CIV scheme itself uses leverage to enhance the co-investment returns
option_c: No, because co-investment within the AIF structure is prohibited for all categories
option_d: No, because the CIV co-investment route is open only to Category I and Category II AIFs

title: An investor approaches an AIF directly, without any distributor. How m
question_text: An investor approaches an AIF directly, without any distributor. How must the AIF onboard them?

options.text: Through the Direct Plan, which must not carry any distribution or placement fee
Through the regular plan, charging the standard placement fee to meet the AIF's costs
Through whichever plan the Manager selects for the investor at its own discretion
Only after appointing a distributor of record to receive the trail commission

explanation: The Direct Plan is mandatory for investors who arrive without a distributor and must not carry distribution or placement fees. Charging such an investor a placement fee, or routing them through a distributor, is a breach of the direct-plan framework.

title: An AIF treats its investment committee as an external advisory panel a
question_text: An AIF treats its investment committee as an external advisory panel and assumes only the Manager bears liability for approved deals. Where is the error?

IC members are equally responsible as the Manager for decisions, external members included
Liability shifts entirely onto the investment committee, fully relieving the Manager

explanation: The Master Circular places investment-committee members on the same liability footing as the Manager for investment decisions and compliance. Constituting the IC does not offload the Manager's liability, and external membership does not dilute it — it shares it.

title: A Manager disclosed all known conflicts in the placement memorandum at
question_text: A Manager disclosed all known conflicts in the placement memorandum at launch and treats that as discharging its conflicts obligation for the fund's life. Is that correct?

No, since conflicts of interest are outright prohibited and cannot be disclosed away
No, since conflicts must be disclosed as they arise and mitigated throughout the business

explanation: Reg. 21 imposes a continuing fiduciary duty: disclose conflicts as and when they arise and monitor and mitigate them throughout the business. A one-time PPM disclosure at launch does not discharge an ongoing obligation.

title: Within what timeline must an AIF's Compliance Test Report be submitted
question_text: Within what timeline must an AIF's Compliance Test Report be submitted, and to whom is the review loop directed?

Within ninety days of each quarter-end, reported directly to the fund's investors only
Within fifteen days of every investment decision, submitted to the merchant banker
Within thirty days of the AIF's date of registration, as a one-time filing only

explanation: The CTR is an annual compliance self-test filed within thirty days of the financial year-end; the trustee or sponsor intimates observations to the manager within thirty days, and the manager cures within fifteen days. It is separate from routine SI-Portal reporting.

title: Which statement correctly distinguishes an AIF's transparency duty fro
question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes an AIF's transparency duty from its reporting duty?

Transparency is continuous disclosure to investors; reporting is periodic filing to SEBI
Transparency is owed only to SEBI, while the reporting duty is owed only to investors
Both are one-time obligations, each discharged at the scheme's first close and no later

explanation: Reg. 22 transparency runs continuously to investors (material information, fees, actions); the reporting duty is periodic filing to SEBI via the SI Portal and the annual CTR. They are different audiences and different cadences, commonly conflated.

title: An AIF proposes to appoint as its independent valuer a firm that is a
question_text: An AIF proposes to appoint as its independent valuer a firm that is a subsidiary of the Manager but holds an IBBI valuer registration and has ten years' experience. Is the appointment valid?

Yes, because a Manager's own subsidiary is best placed to understand the portfolio
No, because the valuer must not be an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee
No, because the valuer must instead be a subsidiary of a credit rating agency in all cases

title: At what point does an asset-level valuation movement become a reportab
question_text: At what point does an asset-level valuation movement become a reportable event to investors?

options.text: Where two consecutive valuations of the asset deviate by more than 20%, or the method changes
Where there is any deviation at all, however small, between two consecutive valuations of the asset
Only where the fund's overall net asset value falls by more than fifty per cent
Only at final close, when all of the scheme's assets are revalued together

explanation: The Master Circular treats an asset-level deviation of more than twenty per cent between consecutive valuations, or a change in methodology, as material and reportable to investors with reasons. A methodology change triggers reporting independently of the percentage.

option_d: Only at final close, when all of the scheme's assets are revalued together

title: In which situation does the requirement to maintain pro-rata rights am
question_text: In which situation does the requirement to maintain pro-rata rights among investors NOT apply?

options.text: Where the Manager simply prefers to give a large investor priority over the returns
Where the scheme is a Category III fund, for which pro-rata rights never apply
Where the investor concerned has held its units for a period of less than one year
Where an investor is excused or excluded from the investment, or has defaulted on a call

explanation: The pro-rata requirement yields only in named cases: an investor excused or excluded from that investment, or one who has defaulted on its pro-rata contribution. Manager preference, category, or holding period are not recognised exceptions.

option_d: Where an investor is excused or excluded from the investment, or has defaulted on a call

title: What did the five-hundred-crore corpus threshold do in the demateriali
question_text: What did the five-hundred-crore corpus threshold do in the dematerialisation framework?

It sequenced the roll-out, bringing larger funds into mandatory demat crediting first
It set the minimum corpus that a scheme must hold in order to be registered
It capped the amount that any single investor may hold in dematerialised form

explanation: The corpus threshold phased the demat crediting roll-out — larger funds first, smaller funds on a later date. It is a sequencing device, not a permanent exemption, and is unrelated to the minimum-corpus registration gate.

title: A director insists SEBI cannot inspect the fund because it has neither
question_text: A director insists SEBI cannot inspect the fund because it has neither alleged wrongdoing nor given the usual notice. Assess this.

Correct as to notice: the ten-day notice period can never lawfully be dispensed with
Wrong on both: inspection may be suo motu and may, under Reg. 31(2), proceed without notice
Wrong only on the allegation point; the ten-day notice is otherwise mandatory always

explanation: Inspection may be initiated suo motu, on information or on complaint — no allegation is needed to begin. title: During an inspection, who bears the duty to produce documents and coop
question_text: During an inspection, who bears the duty to produce documents and cooperate with the Inspecting Authority?

Only the compliance officer, treated as the single designated point of contact for the regulator
Only the trustee of the fund, in the case of a trust-form AIF being inspected
Only external parties such as the custodian, and not the fund's own officers

explanation: Reg. 32 casts the duty widely: every officer and any associated person holding relevant information — expressly including the manager — must produce records and cooperate, and may be examined on oath. Confining the duty to the compliance officer is a common and serious error.

title: A close-ended scheme cannot sell certain investments due to lack of li
question_text: A close-ended scheme cannot sell certain investments due to lack of liquidity at the end of its tenure. Which route is available, and on what investor threshold?

Transfer the affected assets onto the Manager's own book at their last carrying value

Continue holding the assets with no investor approval, given that the tenure has ended
